(3.7)

The transition operator should be interpreted via Kronecker deltas
\delta^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}
(see appendix
B
for full details of the Young transition operators etc. and in particular (
B.3
) for the interpretation in terms of
\delta^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}
).
Then using (
3.3
) we write out (
3.5
) as

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\prime\gamma}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}

\displaystyle=\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{i,1}\right)_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}\,.

(3.8)

and hence read off the independent weight-shifting operators
\mathcal{D}:{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\mapsto{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}
with
|{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}|=|{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}|-1
from (
3.2
) and (
3.5
) as

\displaystyle(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\coloneq(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}}=X^{{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{i,1}\right)^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}\,,

(3.9)

consisting of a multiplicative operator
X
together with a Young transition operator
\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{1,i}
which ensures that
\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(i)}={\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}(1)
.
The counting of independent cases is the same as the number of ways of subtracting a box from the Young diagram
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
, which for a generic representation in the
SL(2m)
case would be
m
--- one at the end of each row.

11
11

11

For a non generic case, we can delete a box at the bottom right of each rectangle consisting of a maximal number of rows of equal length in the Young diagram.

This counting accounts for precisely half the total number of weight-shifting operators which should be
2m
, the dimension of the fundamental representation
\Phi
.

The other, less trivial way to construct operators from
\Phi
and
\mathcal{O}
is using the momentum operator
p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}
.
For this we write the ansatz

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}^{\prime\gamma}=\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime\gamma}

\displaystyle=\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\left(a_{0}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+a_{1}\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+a_{2}\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}\mathcal{O}_{{\mathfrak{b}}{\mathfrak{a}}_{2}\dots,\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+a_{3}\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{a}}_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}{\mathfrak{b}}{\mathfrak{a}}_{3}\dots\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+\dots\right)

\displaystyle=\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\left(a_{0}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}a_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}\ p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}\right)\,.

(3.10)

where
{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}
is the Young tableau obtained from
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
by adding one box corresponding to the new index
{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}
.
The transition operator
\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}
first projects the indices
\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}
of
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}

together with the new index
{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}

according to the corresponding Young tableau
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}(i)
, with
{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}
in the new box, and then transforms this into the lexicographically ordered form (see (
3.6
) but this time from
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}(i)
to
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}(1)
).
The Young symmetriser
\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}
projects the indices
{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}
and
{\mathfrak{b}}
, according to Young tableau
{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(j)
which has the last index
{\mathfrak{b}}
in the extra box.
Here, it is not necessary to further transition to the fully lexicographically ordered case as the index is being contracted.
So completely explicitly, the term in the sum written out with indices is given by

\displaystyle\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}\ p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}=\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}\right)^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\ p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}\ .

(3.11)

Note
\Pi
and
\bar{\Pi}
are denoted differently to emphasise that they act independently of each other: on
GL(m|n)_{L}
and
GL(m|n)_{R}
representation spaces, respectively.

The number of terms inside the sum in (
3.2.1
) corresponds to the number of different ways that a box can be added to
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
.
Crucially, the complexity of the weight-shifting operator does not depend on the Young diagram being acted upon (i.e.
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}\mapsto{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}
in the example above) but rather on the representation on the opposite side (
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
). Since
GL(m|n)
Young diagrams fit into a thick hook of height
m
and length
n
(
2.12
), there are at most
m+n
positions for a new box. Thus, the number of terms in the WSO is limited by the dimension of the superspace. For example, the sum in (
3.2.1
) will have at most 2 terms in 4D (
m=2,n=0
), at most 3 in 4D
\mathcal{N}=2
(
m=2,n=1
), and at most 4 in 4D
\mathcal{N}=4
(
m=2,n=2
).

The coefficients
a_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}
in (
3.2.1
) and (
3.16
) are fixed by demanding
k\mathcal{O}^{\prime}=0
, using the commutator relations (
A.8
), schematically
[k,p]=m_{L}+m_{R}
,
[k,m_{L}]=k
.
Explicitly, applying
k^{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}
to (
3.2.1
) we obtain

\displaystyle k^{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime\gamma}

\displaystyle=\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\left(a_{0}(m{-}n)\delta_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\Phi^{\mathfrak{c}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}a_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}\ \left(\delta_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}^{{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}(m_{L})^{{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}+\delta_{\mathfrak{b}}^{{\mathfrak{c}}}(m_{R})_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}^{\ {\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\right)\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}\right)

\displaystyle=\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\left(a_{0}(m{-}n)\delta_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\Phi^{\mathfrak{c}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}+\Phi^{\mathfrak{b}}\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}a_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}\ \delta_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}^{{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\delta_{\mathfrak{b}}^{{\mathfrak{c}}}\left(B_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(i)}+B_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}\!(j)}\right)\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}\right),

(3.12)

where to get the second line we used (
2.19
) and (
2.22
).

Now we use the following key property of Hermitian Young Projectors (HYPs)

\displaystyle\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in\Box\otimes{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}=\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{1}\,,

(3.13)

which is explained in detail in appendix
B
. Here on the RHS is a HYP which only permutes the indices
\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}
of
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
, leaving the single index
{\mathfrak{b}}
untouched. Thus if we set the coefficients

\displaystyle a_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}=c_{0}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)},\qquad c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}=-\frac{1}{B_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j)}+B_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}}=\frac{1}{\gamma+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j)}+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}}\,,

(3.14)

where
c_{0}=(m{-}n)a_{0}
, then
the sum over Young tableaux in (
3.12
) reduces to (
3.13
) and the entire sum in (
3.12
) reduces to (minus) the first term (the resulting projector
\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{1}
can be pulled through to hit
\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma}
giving the identity). Thus, with the coefficients (
3.14
) we indeed obtain a good primary operator
\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime\gamma}
.

The corresponding weight-shifting operator is then derived by writing (
3.2.1
) in the form of (
3.2
). This is straightforwardly done by extracting
\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}
from
\Phi^{\mathfrak{c}}(X)=X^{{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}
to directly obtain

\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\prime\gamma}=c_{0}\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\left(\bar{W}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}+X^{\mathfrak{b}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\!\!\!\!\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}\!\!\!\!c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\right)\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}^{\gamma},

(3.15)

from which one obtains the weight-shifting operator
\bar{\mathcal{D}}:{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}\mapsto{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}
such that
|{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}|=|{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}|+1
, given by

\displaystyle(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}\coloneq(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}\coloneq c_{0}\left(\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}\left(\bar{W}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}+X^{\mathfrak{b}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\!\!\!\!\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}\!\!\!\!c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\right)\,,

(3.16)

with the coefficients
c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}
given in (
3.14
).
As with the previous weight-shifting operator, in the
(m,0)
case and for generic
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
we see that there will be precisely
m
of these, thus we have accounted for all
2m
weight-shifting operators arising from the fundamental representation
\Phi
.

3.2.2
From the coset to the Grassmannian

The weight-shifting operator (
3.16
), and hence the resulting operator
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}
(
3.2.1
), appear to depend on all the coset variables (
2.2
) and (
2.4
).
But we know that since it is primary it must be rewritable in
a way independent of
W,\bar{W}
by using identities (
2.1
) (see section
2.2.2
and appendix
C
).
So we wish to derive weight-shifting operators depending explicitly on
X_{i},{\bar{X}}_{i}
only i.e. directly on the Grassmannian.

In this section, we show how this works with relevant simple examples, which we will use in applications to blocks in section
5
. The procedure of explicitly deriving the Grassmannian weight-shifting operator from the coset one gets increasingly cumbersome the more terms it has. Thus, in section
3.2.3
, we will show an elegant and simple derivation of the
Grassmannian form of the fundamental weight-shifting operator
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
, capable of acting on any unitary irreducible
SL(2m|2n)
representation
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
.

Scalar example.

Suppose we act on a scalar primary
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}
with no indices. Then the sum in (
3.15
) has only one term, and the coefficient (
3.14
)
c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}}=c_{\Box,\Box}
for a single box is just
1/\gamma
, so (
3.15
) reduces to

{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime\gamma}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}=c_{0}\left(\bar{W}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}+\frac{1}{\gamma}X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}\right)\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}\,.

(3.17)

Then, using the expression for
p=\bar{W}\partial_{X}-\partial_{{\bar{X}}}W
in (
2.23
) we have

\displaystyle{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime\gamma}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}

\displaystyle=c_{0}\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}(\bar{W}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\bar{W}\partial_{X}X-\frac{1}{\gamma}\partial_{\bar{X}}WX)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}

\displaystyle=-\frac{c_{0}}{\gamma}\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}\left(\partial_{\bar{X}}-\gamma\bar{W}-\partial_{\bar{X}}\bar{X}\bar{W}-\bar{W}\partial_{X}X\right)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}\,,

(3.18)

where we used
WX=\mathbb{I}-\bar{X}\bar{W}
(
2.1
) to get the second line. Firstly, note that
\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{\bar{X}}\equiv m_{R}
and
m_{R}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}=-\gamma_{R}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}
(
2.2.1
). Then, the above can be written in a manifestly Grassmannian (
\bar{W},W
independent) form by using the following identity
12
12

12

The simplest way to derive this is by acting on an insertion of generic scalar correlator
\prod_{i}g_{1i}^{\gamma_{L}^{i}}g_{i1}^{\gamma_{R}^{i}}
, where
\gamma_{L,R}=\sum_{i}\gamma_{L,R}^{i}
.

(\bar{W}\partial_{X}X)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}=-\frac{\gamma_{L}}{\gamma_{R}}\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}-\frac{1}{\gamma_{R}}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X}X)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}-\gamma_{L}\bar{W}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}.

(3.19)

Then, by noting that
\gamma_{L}+\gamma_{R}=\gamma
, equation (
3.17
) simplifies to

\displaystyle{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime\gamma}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}=-\frac{c_{0}}{\gamma_{R}}\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}(\partial_{\bar{X}}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X}X)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}\,.

(3.20)

By comparing with (
3.2
), the above defines a weight-shifting operator
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
transforming in the antifundamental
\overline{\Phi}
, which acts on a coset scalar field
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}
by adding a dotted index (so maps
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}=\bullet\mapsto{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}=\Box
) as follows (fixing
c_{0}=-\gamma_{R}
)

(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}=(\partial_{\bar{X}}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X}X)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}.

(3.21)

There is a subtle point here. Recall from section
2.2
that, as a consequence of the symmetry group having unit determinant, the charges
\gamma_{L}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma+\tilde{\gamma})
and
\gamma_{R}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma-\tilde{\gamma})
, which count the homogeneity in
X
and
{\bar{X}}
, respectively, are not good quantum numbers. This is why the operators are labelled by
\gamma
alone. In particular, we have that two different
GL(2m|2n)
representations
(\gamma_{L},\gamma_{R})
and
(\gamma_{L}^{\prime},\gamma_{R}^{\prime})
are equivalent representations of
SL(2m|2n)
if
\gamma_{L}+\gamma_{R}=\gamma_{L}^{\prime}+\gamma_{R}^{\prime}
. Related to this was the fact that the coset variables
X,{\bar{X}},W,\bar{W}
were constrained by the unit determinant constraint.
Thus, in principle, we have to be careful when we differentiate as it can be inconsistent with this constraint. What we learn from (
3.21
) is that the only result of making different choices for
\gamma_{L},\gamma_{R}
arises in the overall normalisation (which we removed by setting
c_{0}=-\gamma_{R}
). We conclude that we can make any choice of
\gamma_{R}
with
\gamma_{L}=\gamma-\gamma_{R}
(apart from
\gamma_{R}=0
) to obtain the same weight-shifting operator, as long as we are consistent throughout the calculation.

Note further that this weight-shifting operator can be simplified further.
If we choose
\gamma_{L}=0
, this operator can be given in terms of
{\bar{X}}
only (independent of
X
) and thus (
3.21
) simplifies to

(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}=\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\ .

(3.22)

General right-handed chiral example.

Before moving to the completely general case we first consider briefly the case where the left-hand representation is still a singlet, but the right-hand one is non-trivial, that is, a chiral field
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\bullet,{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\equiv\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}
. This proceeds very similarly to the singlet case above (
3.17
) but with the addition of the Young symmetriser
\Pi_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}
.
All in all, we derive the Grassmannian (
W,\bar{W}
independent) weight-shifting operator which acts on a chiral field
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\bullet,{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
by adding a box to
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
as follows

\displaystyle(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}=-\frac{c_{0}}{\gamma_{R}+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}}\left(\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}},\qquad\qquad{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}\coloneq(\partial_{\bar{X}}+\frac{1}{\gamma+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}}\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X}X)_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}.

(3.23)

We will again make the choice of overall normalisation of the coset space weight-shifting operator
c_{0}
in order to remove the normalisation in front of the Grassmannian weight-shifting operator,
c_{0}=-(\gamma_{R}+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)})
. We will fix this normalisation in the general case later (see (
4.10
)).

As for the scalar case, we can ensure that
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\bullet,{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
is independent of
X
since all open indices only depend on
{\bar{X}}
, in which case the second term vanishes and we are left with the remarkably simple differential operator

\displaystyle{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}=(\partial_{\bar{X}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}.

(3.24)

3.2.3
Direct derivation on the Grassmannian

In the previous subsection we showed (in the singlet and chiral cases) how the coset space weight-shifting operators can be given directly on the Grassmannian where they have a particularly simple form.
In this section, we will derive this form for the weight-shifting operators directly on the Grassmannian without first going through the coset space description.

Firstly, note that
(\partial_{X})^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}
and
(\partial_{\bar{X}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}
already transform correctly as operators (
2.24
) with one additional
{\mathfrak{a}}
or
{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}
index. Thus, after appropriate young projection, the final result transforms in a new representation of the Levi subgroup. Moreover, with the perspective outlined in appendix
C
, where
k
is a measure of
W,\bar{W}
dependence, the derivatives
\partial_{X}
,
\partial_{{\bar{X}}}
commute with
k
. Thus they naively look like good weight-shifting operators by themselves. However, they are not well-defined operators on the Grassmannian because they do not preserve the hypersurface
X{\bar{X}}=0
. Indeed,

\partial_{X}{}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{a}}}(X{\bar{X}})^{{\mathfrak{b}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}=\delta^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}\neq 0\,,\qquad\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}(X{\bar{X}})^{{\mathfrak{b}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}=\delta^{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\neq 0\,.

Thus, to derive Grassmannian weight-shifting operators, we need to find a differential operator that preserves the orthogonality constraint
X{\bar{X}}=0
.
13
13

13

Note the similarities with the ideal constraint of
[
14
]
.

The fundamental weight-shifting operator which preserves the orthogonality constraint is:

\displaystyle\left(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}=\left(\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}\bar{D}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}},\qquad\bar{D}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}\coloneq(\partial_{\bar{X}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}+\!\!\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in\Box\otimes{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}(X)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{1,j}(\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}.

(3.25)

where the coefficients are in (
3.14
).

To obtain this we wrote down (
3.25
) as an ansatz with arbitrary coefficients
c
, inspired by intuition gained from both the singlet and chiral results derived in the previous subsection as well as the form of the ansatz (
3.16
) in the coset space. We then imposed the constraint
X\bar{X}=0
to fix the coefficients
c
.

The constraint
X\bar{X}=0
is implemented as follows

\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\left(f(X,{\bar{X}})\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\right)|_{X{\bar{X}}=0}=0,

(3.26)

where
f
is a function in the ideal generated by
X\bar{X}
.
It is enough to take a linear term in
X{\bar{X}}
, so
f=(X{\bar{X}})^{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\mathcal{T}_{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}(X,{\bar{X}})
, where
{\mathcal{T}}
is non-singular at
X\bar{X}=0
.

Then, inserting (
3.25
) into (
3.26
) and setting
X\bar{X}=0
we get

\displaystyle 0={\mathcal{T}}_{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}}_{1,i}\left(\delta_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}X^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}+\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in\Box\otimes{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(i),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(j)}(X)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{1,j}\left((m_{L})^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}\delta^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}+(m_{R})^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\ {\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}\delta^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\mathfrak{b}}\right)\right)\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}\,,

(3.27)

where we have simply commuted
(\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}
past
(X\bar{X})^{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}
which gives

\displaystyle[(\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}},(X\bar{X})^{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}]=2(m-n)\delta^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\mathfrak{b}}\delta^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}+(m_{L})^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}\delta^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}+(m_{R})^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\ {\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}\delta^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\mathfrak{b}}\ ,

(3.28)

and since
\mathcal{T}
transforms as dictated by its indices (i.e. (
2.24
) with
\gamma=0
) we have that

\displaystyle\left((m_{L})^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}\delta^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}+(m_{R})^{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}_{\ {\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}\delta^{\mathfrak{c}}_{\mathfrak{b}}\right)\mathcal{T}_{{\mathfrak{c}}{\dot{\mathfrak{c}}}}=-2(m-n)\mathcal{T}_{{\mathfrak{b}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}},

(3.29)

precisely cancelling the constant term in (
3.28
).
From (
3.27
), the process is identical as in the coset calculation starting with (
3.12
)
and hence yielding the same coefficients (
3.14
).
Note from (
3.28
) (and similar commutators), that we obtain the algebra
\mathfrak{sl}(2m|2n)
if we identify
p=\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X}
and
k=X\bar{X}

and add a constant to the
m_{L},m_{R}
. This is reminiscent of the representation of the conformal group in spinor helicity space
[
79
]
(with
k
and
p
swapping roles). It is interesting to note that, with this new perspective, the primary constraint
[k,\mathcal{D}]=0
is equivalent to the constraint (
3.26
).

As a final note, the above result can be derived by acting on
N
-point functions. Weight-shifting operators are in practice used on such functions and hence this is a natural approach.
We simply have to examine how
(X_{1}{\bar{X}}_{1})^{{\mathfrak{a}}{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}
(with the upper indices contracted locally) can appear in a correlation function involving an operator
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}}
at point 1. The only objects that the local indices in
X_{1}{\bar{X}}_{1}
can be contracted against are
\hat{X}_{i1},\hat{X}_{1i}
for some other points
i
. Such a term can only ever appear in the form

\displaystyle(\hat{X}_{j1}X_{1}\bar{X}_{1}X_{1i})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}_{j}{\mathfrak{b}}_{i}}f^{{\mathfrak{b}}_{i}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}_{j}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}}=0\,,

(3.30)

where
f
is an
N
-point structure (as constructed in section
2.3
).
As we show in appendix
A
, this implies all other identities that can arise from the orthogonality constraint, such as the three-point identity
Y_{123}+Y_{132}=0
.
Applying our ansatz (
3.25
) to (
3.30
) yields the expected result for the coefficients (
3.14
).

{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}=\bullet
(the singlet representation) leads to the operators we derived from the coset in section
3.2.2
.

{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
. This will be

5
. Consider acting on a chiral field
\mathcal{O}_{\Box,\bullet}^{\gamma}\equiv\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}
as an illustrative example, we have that

\begin{split}{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}&=\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}+\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}\in\left\{\hbox to10.3pt{\vbox to5.3pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.15pt\lower-0.15pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}

(3.32)

Explicitly (anti)symmetrising the indices in the above equation can be written

{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}=\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma^{2}-1}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}-\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}-1}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{b}}}.

(3.33)

This weight-shifting operator will be used for computing quarter-BPS 4D
\mathcal{N}=4
superconformal blocks in section
5
.
The above computation can be straightforwardly generalised to the general rectangular case
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}=[\lambda^{\mu}]
(
\mu
rows of length
\lambda
) using

(3.34)

where the bigger box denotes the rectangle
[\lambda^{\mu}]
. All in all, the explicit weight-shifting operator acting on a general rectangular antichiral field
\mathcal{O}_{[\lambda^{\mu}],\bullet}^{\gamma}\equiv\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}}
, where
{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}=\Pi^{[\lambda^{\mu}]}_{1}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}\dots{\mathfrak{a}}_{\lambda^{\mu}}
, is

\begin{split}{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}}&=\partial_{{\bar{X}}}{}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}}+\frac{2\gamma+\lambda-\mu}{2(\gamma+\lambda)(\gamma-\mu)}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}}}\\
&\quad\ -\frac{\lambda+\mu}{2(\gamma+\lambda)(\gamma-\mu)}\Pi^{[\lambda^{\mu}]}_{1}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{2}\dots{\mathfrak{a}}_{\lambda^{\scriptscriptstyle\mu}}{\mathfrak{b}}},\end{split}

(3.35)

where in the last line,
\Pi^{[\lambda^{\mu}]}_{1}
is a Young symmetriser of the indices
{\mathfrak{a}}_{1},\dots,{\mathfrak{a}}_{\lambda^{\scriptscriptstyle\mu}}
only (hence why we wrote
X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}
contracting the
{\mathfrak{b}}
index to the right of
\Pi
and not to its left).

3.2.4
Acting on non-unitary representations

So far, we have only considered weight-shifting operators arising from the tensor product of
\Phi
with unitary irreps
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
. We found that this led to
X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}
which acts by contracting an index
{\mathfrak{a}}
, i.e. removing a box from
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
, and to
{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}
which acts by adding an index
{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}
, i.e adding a box to
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
.
However, there is an entire class of operators associated with
\Phi
that we will use but have not considered yet: those acting on representations with upper indices. Recall that this difference is not present in non-supersymmetric theories as representations with upper and lower indices are related by the totally antisymmetric tensor
\epsilon_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}\dots{\mathfrak{a}}_{m}}
of
SL(m)
.
While we will not directly act on this kind of representations as they are non-unitary reps of
SU(m,m|2n)
when
m,n\neq 0

[
62
]
, they will still appear in intermediate steps of calculations even when we initially act on a unitary irrep.

Let us denote such a representation by swapping the position of the representation labels
\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\gamma}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\equiv\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\gamma}^{{\underline{\mathfrak{a}}},{\underline{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}
. Then, as before, we want to find operators

\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}}_{\gamma}\in\Phi\otimes\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{\gamma},

(3.36)

which lead to weight-shifting operators transforming in
\overline{\Phi}
.
By following the same process as before, we arrive at a very similar result

\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}

\displaystyle=\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{1,i}\left(X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\right),

\displaystyle\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}

\displaystyle={\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(1)\,,

(3.37)

\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\Phi^{\mathcal{A}}{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{i,1}\left(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\right),

\displaystyle\qquad\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(i)}

\displaystyle={\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(1)\,.

Unlike in the lower index case,
X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}
now adds an index
{\mathfrak{a}}
to
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
and symmetrises it accordingly, and
{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}
(
3.25
) now contracts an index
{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}
from
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
as picked by
\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{1,i}
.

The derivation of the differential weight-shifting operator (
3.37
) follows the same process outlined in the previous sections with the key difference of acting on upper indices by removing a box. In particular, the ansatz for
{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}
above is as follows

\displaystyle{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}=(\partial_{\bar{X}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}+\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\otimes\Box}\tilde{c}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}(j),{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(i)}(\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{1,j}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}},

(3.38)

where
i,j
label the specific standard Young tableau, giving the information of the position of the
{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}},{\mathfrak{b}}
indices being contracted, respectively.
The solution to the ansatz follows similarly to the unitary case (
3.14
) and is given by

\tilde{c}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(j),{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(i)}=\frac{1}{\gamma-2(m-n)-C_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}(j)}-C_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(i)}}.

(3.39)

3.3
General weight-shifting operators

In the previous subsection, we derived fundamental (
\Phi
)
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators (
3.9
), (
3.25
) and (
3.14
) from tensor products of the fundamental
\Phi
of
SL(2m|2n)
and a field
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
. They are
SL(2m|2n)
-covariant, transforming in the antifundamental
\overline{\Phi}
, and are made of a multiplicative or differential operator with an accompanying permutation operator. The same step by step process can be followed to derive weight-shifting operators
\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}}
,
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
arising from tensor products of the antifundamental
\overline{\Phi}
of
SL(2m|2n)
, which will instead transform in
\Phi
.
14
14

14

We will always denote a weight-shifting operator by the representation they transform in, which is the dual of the finite representation they arise from.

All in all, the results for our (anti)fundamental
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators acting on unitary irreducible representations
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
of the superconformal group
SU(m,m|2n)
by mapping
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L,R}\mapsto{\underline{\lambda}}_{L,R}^{\prime}
are

\displaystyle\Phi:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} (\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}\coloneq(\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}})^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}&={\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}^{\prime}}\left(\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{i,1}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}^{\prime}},\qquad\quad\hskip-4.55244pt&\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(i)}&={\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(1),\\
(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\coloneq(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}})^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}}&=\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{1,i}\right)^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}D_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}^{\mathcal{A}},\qquad\quad&\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}&={\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(1),\end{aligned}

(3.40)

\displaystyle\overline{\Phi}:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} (\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\coloneq(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}}&=X^{{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{i,1}\right)^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}},\qquad\quad&\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(i)}&={\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(1),\\
(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}\coloneq\left(\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}&=\left(\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}}_{1,i}\right)^{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}^{\prime}}\bar{D}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}},\qquad\quad&\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}&={\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(1),\end{aligned}

where (
3.25
)

\displaystyle\bar{D}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}

\displaystyle\coloneq(\partial_{\bar{X}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{A}}+X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\in\Box\otimes{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{j}(\partial_{\bar{X}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\,,

(3.41)

\displaystyle D_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}^{\mathcal{A}}

\displaystyle\coloneq(\partial_{X}){}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{a}}}+{\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\sum_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}\in{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}\otimes\Box}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}(i),{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}(j)}\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}}_{i}(\partial_{{\bar{X}}}\partial_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}\,,

(3.42)

and (
3.14
)

c_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(j),{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}=\frac{1}{\gamma+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(j)}+C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}}.

(3.43)

The indices
i,j
on the Young projectors
\Pi
simply specify the Young tableau with given shape
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L/R},{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L/R}
and are uniquely specified by the conditions on removing the last box. In practice, the last box denotes the index being contracted/added.
See appendix
B
for details on Young diagrams, tableaux and projectors.
Note that there is no explicit
m,n
dependence in the weight-shifting operators and its presence is only in the size of
{\mathfrak{a}}
and
\mathcal{A}
indices and in the allowed non vanishing shape of the Young diagrams
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
and
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}^{\prime}
. One can thus use (
3.40
) to compute quantities in theories with
SL(2m|2n)
symmetry in a unified manner, and fix
m,n
at the end.

General weight-shifting operators
\mathcal{D}_{\Psi}
transforming in a representation
\Psi\in\Phi^{\otimes p}\otimes\overline{\Phi}^{\otimes q}
can be constructed by successive application of the (anti)fundamental weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).
15
15

15

This is automatic for the Grassmannian operators we considered here and follows more generally from the algebra of weight-shifting operators
[
14
]
, reviewed in section
4
.

In this section, we will show how such differential operators shift the weights of 4D
\mathcal{N}=0,2,4
multiplets as well as their interaction with shortening conditions.
For this, we ignore the open
SL(2m|2n)
indices, which should be understood as being contracted by different weight-shifting operators acting on other points of an
N
-point structure.

\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
(

)

Note that contracting and antisymmetrising a Weyl spinor index in 4D are equivalent operations.

An advantage of our formalism is that the same operator has two different actions, which only depend on Young symmetriser
\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}
. Moreover, the differential operators
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
often simplify substantially to simply
\partial_{X}
and
\partial_{{\bar{X}}}
together with a subsequent symmetriser.
17
17

17

Indeed, since
X
and
{\bar{X}}
are not independent, many
N
-point structures can be written independently of one variable, simplifying the differential WSOs.

(3.47)

See appendix
D
for the full correspondence between coset space representations and superconformal multiplets.
In particular, the diagram (
3.45
) can be completed by adding an arbitrary long column in which any added box contributes to the
SU(2)
part of the full
U(2)

R
-symmetry representation. The remaining
\mathbb{C}^{*}
charge corresponds to the difference between left and right Young diagrams and thus any shift of one side will shift it.
All other types of multiplets can be accessed by acting with the dual weight-shifting operator
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
.

4D
\mathcal{N}=4
multiplets.

Because
SL(4|4)
is not semi-simple, there is an additional constraint that multiplets must satisfy, indicating that they are actually representations of
PSL(4|4)
. In particular, 4D
\mathcal{N}=4
multiplets are described by
SL(m|n)\times SL(m|n)
representations with the same number of boxes on each side. This is described in detail in appendix
D
. Thus, to map between representations, it is necessary to apply differential operators in the adjoint of
\mathfrak{sl}(2m|2n)
given by tensor products of (
3.40
). We focus on
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{B}}
which gives physical reps starting from the scalar rep.
The number of possible different operations grows rapidly so we only show the first two steps, together with their translation to the notation of
[
80
]
, where 4D
\mathcal{N}=4
superconformal multiplets are written as

S\bar{S}[\ell,\bar{\ell}]^{(R_{1},R_{2},R_{3})}_{\Delta}\,.

(3.48)

The successive application of the adjoint weight-shifting operator
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{B}}
on the first few
\mathcal{N}=4
multiplets is as follows

(3.49)

where the dashed arrows indicate continuation. In general, for two Young diagrams
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
and
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
with
N
and
M
distinct rectangles, respectively, there will be
(N+1)\times(M+1)
possible operations, that is, arrows coming out of their corresponding node.
Using table

Note that as currently written, this is a superconformally covariant object. Indeed, in order to obtain the full physically relevant quantity, we need to contract the
\mathcal{A}

In the next section, we will consider such invariant compositions of weight-shifting operators.

3.4
Conformal fields in the Grassmannian formalism

A nice by-product of the above formalism is in the construction of operators from fundamental scalar fields (
\gamma=1
singlets) which takes a remarkably simple form. One simply applies WSOs,
(\partial_{X})^{\mathcal{A}}{}_{\mathfrak{a}}
, to
\Phi
s (which we
assume to be chiral and depend only on
X
not
{\bar{X}}
)
and
(\bar{\partial}_{X})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}
derivatives to
\bar{\Phi}
s and contract all the
\mathcal{A}
indices. Note that the equation of motion of the fundamental scalar enforces that when acting with derivatives on a single scalar, all indices are automatically symmetrised

\displaystyle\partial^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}{}_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}..\partial^{\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}}{}_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{\lambda}}\Phi=\partial^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}{}_{({\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}..\partial^{\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}}{}_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{\lambda})}\Phi\qquad\qquad\qquad\bar{\partial}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{1}\mathcal{A}_{1}}..\bar{\partial}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\lambda}\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}}\bar{\Phi}=\bar{\partial}_{({\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{1}|\mathcal{A}_{1}|}..\bar{\partial}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\lambda})\mathcal{A}_{\lambda}}\bar{\Phi}\ .

(3.52)

Then we can write any representation (with equal numbers of left and right indices, so e.g. all operators in
\mathcal{N}=4
SYM) in terms of fundamental scalars explicitly as

\displaystyle{\mathcal{O}}^{\gamma_{L},\gamma_{R}}_{\underline{\lambda},\underline{\mu}}=\Pi^{\underline{\lambda}}_{1}\bar{\Pi}^{\underline{\mu}}_{1}\left[\partial^{\lambda_{1}}\Phi_{1}..\partial^{\lambda_{\gamma_{L}}}\Phi_{\gamma_{L}}\ \cdot\ \bar{\partial}^{\mu_{1}}\bar{\Phi}_{1}..\partial^{\mu_{\gamma_{R}}}\bar{\Phi}_{\gamma_{R}}\right]\ .

(3.53)

Here the left and right Young diagrams have row lengths
\underline{\lambda}=[\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\gamma_{L}}]
and
\underline{\mu}=[\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{\gamma_{R}}]
some of which could be vanishing. The scalar fields
\Phi_{i},\bar{\Phi}_{i}
are considered to be all different for full generality, but in a specific situation they will likely have further structure (e.g. adjoint
SU(N)
indices over which we take traces). The operation
\Pi\bar{\Pi}
is a Young projector, projecting the left
{\mathfrak{a}}
indices onto the rep
\underline{\lambda}
and right
{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}
indices onto the rep
\underline{\mu}
. Finally the dot
\cdot
indicates that we contract all
\mathcal{A}
indices together. For this we require that there are equal numbers of
\partial
and
\bar{\partial}
derivatives.

Note the simplicity of this result, even for standard 4D Minkowski space where recall one normally has to write a linear combination of terms with derivatives acting in different places and impose vanishing under special conformal transformations. Here there is always just a single term.

4
Weight-shifting invariants

The goal of this section is to construct
SL(2m|2n)
-invariant compositions of the weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).
The starting point is the algebraic structure that superconformal weight-shifting operators satisfy, i.e. how compositions of these covariant differential operators act, which is closely related to the
SL(2m|2n)
-associativity of tensor products of representations.
Indeed, it takes a similar form to the algebra of
SO(d+1,1)
weight-shifting operators shown in
[
14
]
.
The first consequence of this algebra is a constraining property for constructing weight-shifting invariants known in practice as the
bubble
, which is a realisation of Schur’s lemma.
As we shall see, this implies that such invariants can only be constructed from weight-shifting operators acting at different points, of a correlation function for instance. The algebra of weight-shifting operators also allows us to understand the action of these differential operators on
N
-point functions, which we will show in
4.3
. Then, in section
4.4
, we use this to construct the
SL(2m|2n)
-invariant compositions of superconformal weight-shifting operators.
This then provides the basis for understanding their action on superconformally invariant
N
-point structures and hence superconformal blocks.

4.1
Diagrams and weight-shifting algebra

We will be using a very useful diagrammatic notation for general weight-shifting operators,

\mathcal{D}_{\Psi}
, introduced in
[
14
]
, which we will make extensive use of and which reflects the close relationship between the weight-shifting operators and the tensor product of representations (
3.1
), (
3.2
) (and in turn, three-point functions).
Edges with arrows denote representations, a standard edge for a generic operator, a dashed edge for a scalar (half-BPS) operator and a curly edge for a finite dimensional representation

\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{\bullet,\bullet}
\Psi
.

N

(4.3)

As explained in the previous section, a general weight-shifting operator
\mathcal{D}_{\Psi}
can always be constructed from successive applications of the (anti)fundamental weight-shifting operators,
\mathcal{D}_{\Phi},\mathcal{D}_{\bar{\Phi}}
(
3.40
). In this case, the label in each individual node is not necessary as it is uniquely determined by the initial and final states. For example, for
\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}\mapsto\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
,
|{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}|=1+|{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}|
, there is only one (anti)fundamental weight-shifting operator (
3.40
) that can achieve it:
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
.

The above statement can be made more precise by the algebra of weight-shifting operators, which relates consecutive applications of weight-shifting operators,
\mathcal{D}_{\Phi_{1}}\mathcal{D}_{\Phi_{2}}
, to linear combinations of single weight-shifting operators
\mathcal{D}_{\Psi}
,
\Psi\in\Phi_{1}\otimes\Phi_{2}
, and is represented diagrammatically as

where the small vertex on the RHS is the relevant Clebsch-Gordan coefficient and the object in curly brackets are simply the coefficients in this relation, known as 6
j
symbols for the Lie group
G
. These coefficients are best known for
G=SU(2)
where they describe the crossing between tensor products of different spins in the way depicted in (
4.4
).
Within the
(m,n)
superspace, we are able to extend these ideas to the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-graded Lie group
SL(2m|2n)
and thus obtain superconformal
6j
symbols.

We now consider the properties of weight-shifting operators that follow from the above algebra, as first shown in
[
14
]
, giving explicit realisations using our
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).

4.2
Bubble

If we set
\Phi_{2}=\overline{\Phi}_{1}=\overline{\Phi}
in (
4.4
) and make the whole expression invariant by contracting indices, we get a bubble diagram. The sum on the right-hand side of (
4.4
) will now only have one non-zero term, corresponding to
\Psi=\mathbf{1}
, the trivial representation. This means that
\mathcal{O}
must be equal to
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}
.
18
18

18

Note that this is simply a realisation of Schur’s lemma.

We conclude that the conformally invariant composition of two weight-shifting operators
either vanishes or leaves the representation unchanged. This is known as the bubble and
is summarised by the following equation

{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}=\dim{\Phi}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}&\mathbf{1}\\
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}&\overline{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}^{\prime\prime}\end{array}\right\}\delta_{\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}^{\prime}}\mathcal{O}\ .

Upon first look, this property implies that we cannot perform non-trivial changes to representations. However, in practice, weight-shifting operators are used on correlation functions, i.e. there are more points to apply differential operators at, and thus more ways of constructing non-trivial conformally invariant expressions using weight-shifting techniques, which we will show in section
4.4
.

Let us show that the fundamental and anti-fundamental superconformal weight-shifting operators (
3.40
) satisfy the bubble property (
4.2
).
There are four different combinations to consider:
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}},\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}},\,\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}}
and
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
.

When neither weight-shifting operator is differential, the property
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}\bar{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathcal{A}}=0
is trivially satisfied on both the coset and Grassmannian following directly from
X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}{\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}=0
.
In this case the RHS vanishes, consistent with (
4.2
) since the final representation is always different from the initial one (we apply a right-hand shift followed by a left-hand shift).

The second and third cases are more subtle: if one operator adds an index and the other contracts, there are cases in which the final Young diagram is equal to the initial one and so the combination does not vanish.
We only consider
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
as the conjugate case is very similar.
Now note that, unlike their multiplicative counterparts, differential weight-shifting operators have different forms on the coset (
3.16
) and Grassmannian (
3.40
) and so we consider each case separately. The coset differential operators obey the bubble property more non-trivially:

\displaystyle(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime\prime}_{L}}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}

\displaystyle=c_{0}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{i,1}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{1,j}\bigg(W{}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}+{\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}\sum_{\mu_{R}\in\Box\otimes{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}c_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}(j){\underline{\mu}}_{R}}\bar{\Pi}^{{\underline{\mu}}_{R}}_{k}p_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}\bigg)

\displaystyle=c_{0}X^{{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{i,j}W{}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}=c_{0}\delta_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime\prime}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}\,.

(4.7)

The
i,j,k
are defined by
\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(j)}={\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(1),\ \overline{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}={\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime\prime}_{L}(1),\ \overline{{\underline{\mu}}_{R}(k)}={\underline{\lambda}}_{R}(1)
where the barred tableau is the tableau with the final entry (and its box) removed. Thus

\delta_{i,j}=\delta_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime\prime}}
. In the second equality we used
X\bar{X}=0
and the final equality uses
XW=I
(
2.1
) as well as beautiful properties of Hermitian Young projectors. It is shown explicitly in appendix
B
.

The above composition of WSOs using the Grassmannian form of the WSO
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
(
3.40
) is slightly trickier. The computation is similar to (
4.7
), with
W\rightarrow\partial_{X}
, and thus the second line becomes

\displaystyle(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime\prime}_{L}}(\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}})^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}=\left(\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{i,j}\right)^{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}(X\partial_{X})^{{\mathfrak{b}}^{\prime}}_{\ {\mathfrak{b}}}\mathcal{O}_{\underline{{\mathfrak{a}}},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}=B^{\gamma_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(i)}\delta_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}\ .

(4.8)

The second equality follows from the fact that
\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{i,j}=\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{i,j}\Pi^{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}^{\prime}}_{j}
(which follows from (
B.5
)) after which we can use (
2.19
) to yield
B^{\gamma_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(i)}
multiplied by (
4.7
).

Thus, the coefficient
B^{\gamma_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}\!(i)}
defined by equation (
2.19
) is precisely the
6j
symbol (
4.2
):

\dim\Phi\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\Phi&\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}&\bullet\\
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}&\overline{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}^{\gamma}\end{array}\right\}\equiv B_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}^{\gamma_{L}}=-\gamma_{L}-C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}.

(4.9)

The process is similar for the combination
{\bar{X}}^{\mathcal{A}{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}
.
Note that by comparing (
4.7
) and (
4.9
) we can now fix the normalisation
c_{0}
relating the coset and Grassmannian versions of the weight-shifting operators

D_{{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\mathcal{A}}:\quad c_{0}=-\gamma_{L}-C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L}(i)}\qquad\qquad{\bar{D}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{A}}:\quad c_{0}=-\gamma_{R}-C_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{R}(i)}\,.

(4.10)

Note that this is in complete agreement with the normalisation derived directly in (
3.23
).

Finally, the case where both weight-shifting operators are differential is highly non-trivial.
Because each differential operator always adds a box to the corresponding Young diagram
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}
,
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
(or removes it in the case of non-unitary irreps (
3.38
)), the combination should always vanish by the bubble property.
We include it in its full generality in appendix
E
as it is an instructive application of all the properties of Young projectors, the relations between coset space coordinates, and the coefficients
c_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
of weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).
Here, we will consider an example.

Suppose we act on
\mathcal{O}_{\bullet,\bullet}^{\gamma}
by adding a box to both left and right
GL(m|n)
representations. Without loss of generality, we add an undotted index first by acting with
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}
and then a dotted one with
\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. Then, we claim that the following vanishes

3.40
), the bubble property calculation follows similar steps with
W\mapsto\partial_{X}
,

4.3
Crossing and superconformal
6j
symbols

By swapping one of the finite-dimensional representations
\Phi_{i}
in (
4.4
) by an infinite-dimensional one
\mathcal{O}
, the corresponding node becomes a three-point structure and thus the algebra of weight-shifting operators becomes an equation relating the action of weight-shifting operators at two different insertions. Diagrammatically, this looks like a
crossing

(4.14)

where the coefficients are again
6j
symbols as in (
4.4
), but with the finite representations replaced by infinite-dimensional ones and thus the sum is now over
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{2}\otimes\Phi
. We considered the fundamental representation
\Phi
, which works similarly for the antifundamental
\overline{\Phi}
. The crossing equation for general finite representation
\Psi
follows from successive application of the above equation and/or its antifundamental counterpart as we showed in section
3.3
, which itself follows from (
4.4
).

The crossing diagram above corresponds to

\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1})\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle^{(j)}=\sum_{i,\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{2}}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\mathcal{O}_{2}&\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}&\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{2}\\
\mathcal{O}_{3}&\Phi&\mathcal{O}_{1}\end{array}\right\}_{i}^{j}\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{2})\langle\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle^{(i)}.

(4.15)

This equation provides a new and simple way of computing
SL(2m|2n)

6j
symbols using the weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).

Let us consider a simple example given by
adding an
{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}
index at position 1 to a scalar three-point function
(we use dashed lines to indicate superspace scalars):

\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}(X_{1})\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}(X_{2})\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{3}}(X_{3})\rangle=g_{21}^{\gamma_{12,3}}g_{23}^{\gamma_{23,1}}g_{31}^{\gamma_{31,2}}=\hbox to81.09pt{\vbox to71.66pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 40.54535pt\lower-40.8931pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

, by using the weight-shifting operator
\mathcal{D}^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}=X^{{\mathfrak{a}}}_{\ \mathcal{A}}
.

4.4
Differential basis for
SL(2m|2n)
-invariant structures

Recall that the bubble property (
4.2
) states that
SL(2m|2n)
invariant combinations of weight-shifting operators acting at the same point are unable to change the representation. For this reason, one needs to act at different points in the
N
-point structure in order to perform non-trivial changes in the representations. That is, we want to construct invariant compositions of the weight-shifting operators (
3.40
) given by repeated action of

{\mathfrak{D}}_{ij}\coloneq\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{i})\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_{j}),

(4.21)

which act at two different insertions
X_{i},\,X_{j}
of an
N
-point structure.
The idea then is that for a given third operator
\mathcal{O}_{3}
we can obtain any non-vanishing three-point function
\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle
by acting with appropriate combinations of
{\mathfrak{D}}_{12}
on any other non-vanishing three-point function
\langle\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle
.
In particular we should be able to cover the full space of tensor structures for a given three-point correlator by acting on a possibly unique 3-point function with different combinations of
{\mathfrak{D}}_{12}
’s.

Suppose we act on a three-point function
\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle
with
\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1}):\mathcal{O}_{1}\mapsto\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}
,
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_{2}):\mathcal{O}_{2}\mapsto\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}
. One can use crossing (
4.14
) to better understand the action of
{\mathfrak{D}}_{12}

[
14
]
,

\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1})\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_{2})\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle=\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1})\sum_{i,\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime\prime}}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\mathcal{O}_{1}&\mathcal{O}_{3}&\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime\prime}\\
\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}&\overline{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}_{2}\end{array}\right\}_{i}\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1})\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime\prime}\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle^{(i)},

(4.22)

where on the RHS
\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime\prime}\mapsto\mathcal{O}_{1}
. Then, by the bubble property (
4.2
), only the term
\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}
survives, leading to

\mathcal{D}^{\mathcal{A}}(X_{1})\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{A}}(X_{2})\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle=\dim{\Phi}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}&\mathbf{1}\\
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}&\overline{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}_{1}\end{array}\right\}\sum_{i}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}\mathcal{O}_{1}&\mathcal{O}_{3}&\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}\\
\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}&\overline{\Phi}&\mathcal{O}_{2}\end{array}\right\}_{i}\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle^{(i)},

(4.23)

where the coefficient before the sum is precisely the bubble coefficient
B^{\gamma_{L}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(i)}
(
4.9
)
(with
\mathcal{O}_{1}=\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
,
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}=\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
and
\overline{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}(i)}={\underline{\lambda}}^{\prime}(1)
).
The above results follow straightforwardly using the diagrammatic notation, in particular (
4.2
) and (
4.14
) (see see (
4.25
)).

In practice one can cover the space of different tensor structures on the RHS (labelled by
i
) by choosing different WSOs on the LHS (in practice by applying further weight-shifting operators). Indeed it is then useful to invert this and define a basis of the three-point structures via the differential operators
{\mathfrak{D}}^{[i]}_{12}
. This is known as the
differential
basis, and we will denote it by square brackets
\langle\dots\rangle^{[i]}
as follows

\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle^{[j]}\coloneq{\mathfrak{D}}^{[j]}_{12}\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle.

(4.24)

We will show this inversion explicitly in terms of our
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators (
3.40
) shortly.
In terms of diagrams, we denote the differential basis by a square node

\hbox to74.4pt{\vbox to67.62pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 23.4067pt\lower-33.80885pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-20.07368pt}{22.95802pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}},

(4.25)

where to simplify notation, we label the exchanged finite rep in the differential basis by a square node.

Note that in practice, we always wish to act on a three point function
\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\rangle
which itself has a
unique
tensor structure. If the third operator is symmetric then we can act on the three-point function of that operator with two scalars, which indeed has a unique tensor structure, and in the next subsections we will examine this case explicitly in a number of examples.

For a more general third operator
\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{3}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{L},{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}}
consider
{\underline{\lambda}}={\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\cap{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}
and then pick any irreps
{\underline{\mu}}_{1},{\underline{\mu}}_{2}
such that
{\underline{\lambda}}_{L}\in{\underline{\lambda}}\otimes\mu_{1}
,
{\underline{\lambda}}_{R}\in{\underline{\lambda}}\otimes\mu_{2}
. Then the three-point function
of (anti-)chiral operators
\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\mu}}_{1},\bullet}
and
\mathcal{O}_{\bullet,{\underline{\mu}}_{2}}
with
\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{1},{\underline{\lambda}}_{2}}
will have a unique tensor structure

\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\mu}}_{1},\bullet}\mathcal{O}_{\bullet,{\underline{\mu}}_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{1},{\underline{\lambda}}_{2}}\rangle\sim\hat{X}_{31}^{|{\underline{\mu}}_{1}|}\hat{X}_{23}^{|{\underline{\mu}}_{2}|}Y_{3}^{|{\underline{\lambda}}|}\,.

(4.26)

Thus we will build any three-point function
\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}_{1},{\underline{\lambda}}_{2}}\rangle
by acting with combinations of
{\mathfrak{D}}_{12}^{[i]}
on this.

4.4.1
An illustrative example

Before considering the more general construction, we show a simple explicit example of the differential basis using our
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators (
3.40
).

Let us consider
\langle\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{a}}^{\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{O}_{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}^{\gamma_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}},{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle
. We know from section
2.3
that the space of
SL(2m|2n)
invariant tensor structures is two-dimensional in this case. The two tensor structures in the standard basis are given by

\begin{split}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma}\rangle^{(1)}&=K(\hat{X}_{21})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}(Y_{3}^{|{\underline{\lambda}}|})_{{\underline{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}{\underline{\mathfrak{b}}}},\\
\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma}\rangle^{(2)}&=K(\hat{X}_{23})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{b}}}(\hat{X}_{31})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}(Y_{3}^{|{\underline{\lambda}}|-1})_{{\underline{\dot{\mathfrak{b}}}}{\underline{\mathfrak{b}}}}.\end{split}

(4.27)

We thus expect to be able to construct two different weight-shifting operators which, when applied to the three point function
\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle
, yield linearly independent structures.
The only possible such combinations are

\begin{split}{\mathfrak{D}}^{[1]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}&\coloneq(\hat{X}_{21})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}},\\
{\mathfrak{D}}^{[2]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}&\coloneq(\bar{D}_{2})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}\mathcal{A}}(D_{1})^{\mathcal{A}}_{\ {\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}.\end{split}

(4.28)

Note that in non-supersymmetric cases,
\hat{X}_{ij}\coloneq(X_{ji})^{-1}
can be constructed as a polynomial in
\bar{X}_{i}
and
X_{j}
(multiplied by
g_{ij}
, the inverse determinant of
X_{ji}
)

(\hat{X}_{ji}){}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{j}^{1}{\mathfrak{a}}_{i}^{1}}=\frac{1}{(m-1)!}\times{g_{ji}}\underbrace{(X_{ij}\dots X_{ij})}_{m-1}{}^{{\mathfrak{a}}_{i}^{2}\dots{\mathfrak{a}}_{i}^{m}{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{j}^{2}\dots{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{j}^{m}}{\epsilon_{{\mathfrak{a}}_{i}^{1}\dots{\mathfrak{a}}_{i}^{m}}\bar{\epsilon}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{j}^{1}\dots{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{j}^{m}}}.

(4.29)

In particular, in 4D the combination is simply
X_{12}g_{21}
with spinor indices lowered by epsilon tensors. In a general supersymmetric setting where
m,n\neq 0
, the super determinant is instead non-polynomial. The writing in diagrammatic form in terms of finite reps
\Phi
as in (
4.25
) is then somewhat formal.

We can then verify that the operators (
4.28
) give rise to two linearly independent tensor structures

\begin{split}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle^{[1]}&\equiv(\hat{X}_{21})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle\\
&=\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle^{(1)},\\
\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle^{[2]}&\equiv(\partial_{{\bar{X}}_{2}}\partial_{X_{1}})_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}{\mathfrak{a}}}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle\\
&=c_{1}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle^{(1)}+c_{2}\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}_{{\mathfrak{a}}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}^{\gamma_{3}}\rangle^{(2)},\end{split}

(4.30)

where

c_{1}=\gamma_{12,3}\left(\frac{1}{2}(\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3})-m+n\right),\qquad c_{2}=-(1-\delta_{{\underline{\lambda}},\bullet})(\gamma_{3}+L_{{\underline{\lambda}}}-H_{{\underline{\lambda}}}),

(4.31)

with
\gamma_{ij,k}=(\gamma_{i}+\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{k})/2
. It is then evident that both tensor structures are linearly independent for all
m,n
unless
{\underline{\lambda}}=\bullet
or
\gamma_{3}=-L_{{\underline{\lambda}}}+H_{{\underline{\lambda}}}
.
In terms of graphs we have that

\begin{split}\hbox to107.13pt{\vbox to79.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 55.11421pt\lower-40.2338pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{{}{}}}{{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-51.7812pt}{29.20041pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 20.45 0 C 20.45 2.16 18.7 3.91 16.54 3.91 C 14.37 3.91 12.62 2.16 12.62 0 C 12.62 -2.16 14.37 -3.91 16.54 -3.91 C 18.7 -3.91 20.45 -2.16 20.45 0 Z M 16.54 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{11.95021pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

4.4.2
General construction

As we will see in section
5
, the differential basis is essential for computing blocks.
Thus, we will now give a construction of the differential basis for some families of correlators with our
SL(2m|2n)
weight-shifting operators (
3.40
) which we will later make use of in constructing superblocks.
As usual, we work with unfixed
m,n
so Young diagrams can be arbitrarily large. By fixing
m,n
to cases of interest (e.g. 4D
\mathcal{N}=0,2,4
), the methods we show here can be used to prove the existence of the differential basis in general.

20

20

It was shown for symmetric traceless tensors in
[
13
]
using the embedding space formalism.

\langle\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\mu}},\bullet}\mathcal{O}_{\bullet,{\underline{\mu}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}\rangle
:

Such a correlator has
|{\underline{\mu}}|+1
independent tensor structures (for generic
{\underline{\lambda}}
, that is,
|{\underline{\mu}}|\leq|{\underline{\lambda}}|
). In the standard basis
\langle\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\mu}},\bullet}\mathcal{O}_{\bullet,{\underline{\mu}}}\mathcal{O}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}\rangle^{(k)}
they are given by

Note the similarities with (
2.38
).

K\,\underbrace{\hat{X}_{21}\dots\hat{X}_{21}}_{|{\underline{\mu}}|-k}\ \underbrace{(\hat{X}_{23}\hat{X}_{31})\dots(\hat{X}_{23}\hat{X}_{31})}_{k}\ \underbrace{Y_{3}\dots Y_{3}}_{|{\underline{\lambda}}|-k}\ ,\qquad k=0,1,\dots,|{\underline{\mu}}|.

(4.33)

As shown in the previous subsection, the way to construct the differential basis of tensor structures in the chiral case is by using the two invariant weight-shifting operators
{\mathfrak{D}}^{[1]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}},{\mathfrak{D}}^{[2]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}
(
4.28
) on a three-point correlator with one less index at points 1 and 2.

However if we recurse this process we can instead construct the differential basis by acting on
\langle\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{1}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{2}}\mathcal{O}^{\gamma_{3}}_{{\underline{\lambda}}}\rangle
, which has a single structure. This is what we will be doing when constructing superconformal blocks in section
5
.
So we now need to apply one of the invariant differential operators
{\mathfrak{D}}^{[1]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}},{\mathfrak{D}}^{[2]}_{{\dot{\mathfrak{a}}}_{2}{\mathfrak{a}}_{1}}

4.28
